glossary.definition: Money a company spends on long-lived assets: factories, equipment, data centres, software it capitalises. It is not an expense in the income statement in the year paid (it is depreciated over time) but it is cash out. Free cash flow = operating cash flow − CapEx.
The day-to-day costs of running the business (salaries, rent, marketing, R&D), expensed in the year they occur. Contrast with CapEx.
Cash generated by the business's normal operations in a period, after working-capital changes and before investing or financing flows.
Operating cash flow minus CapEx: the cash left to pay dividends, buy back shares, pay down debt or acquire. Harder to flatter with accounting choices than earnings.
Free cash flow per share divided by the share price (or FCF / market cap). A cash-based alternative to the earnings yield (1 / P/E).
Total sales in a period (the top line), before any costs.
(Revenue − cost of goods sold) / revenue. How much of each euro of sales is left after the direct cost of producing it.
Operating income (EBIT) / revenue: profit from the core business after operating expenses, before interest and tax.
Net income / revenue: what is left for shareholders from each euro of sales after all costs, interest and tax.
Earnings Before Interest and Taxes — operating profit.
Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation. A rough proxy for operating cash generation that ignores CapEx, so it flatters capital-heavy companies.
The yearly non-cash charge that spreads the cost of past CapEx (depreciation) or acquired intangibles (amortisation) over their useful life.
Net income divided by the number of shares. Trailing EPS uses the last 12 months; forward EPS uses analysts' estimate for the next 12 months.
Share price / EPS: how many years of current earnings you pay for. Trailing P/E uses past earnings, forward P/E analysts' estimates. Only comparable within similar businesses.
P/E divided by the expected earnings growth rate (in %). Around 1 is often read as growth priced fairly; it inherits all the uncertainty of the growth estimate.
Share price / book value per share. Book value is assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet; useful for banks and insurers, less so for asset-light companies.
Market cap / revenue. Used for companies without profits yet; ignores margins.
Share price × shares outstanding: what the market values the equity at.
Market cap + debt − cash: the price of the whole business, independent of how it is financed.
Enterprise value divided by EBITDA. A valuation multiple that, unlike P/E, compares companies with different debt levels.
Net income / shareholders' equity: profit generated per euro the owners have in the business. High debt can inflate it.
Net income / total assets: how profitably a company uses everything it owns.
After-tax operating profit / (debt + equity invested). Above the cost of capital means growth creates value.
Total debt / shareholders' equity (Yahoo shows it as a percentage, so 150 = 1.5×). A leverage measure; normal levels differ a lot by sector.
Total debt minus cash. Negative means the company holds more cash than debt (a net cash position).
Current assets / current liabilities: can the company pay what falls due within a year? Below 1 can signal liquidity pressure.
Dividends / net income. Above ~100% means the dividend is paid from more than the year's earnings and may not be sustainable.
Dividends per share over the last (or next) 12 months / current share price.
A company repurchasing its own shares, returning cash to shareholders and raising EPS by reducing the share count.
A durable competitive advantage (brand, network effects, switching costs, cost advantage) that protects a company's returns from competitors.
Fair value is your estimate of what a share is worth; buying well below it leaves a margin of safety against being wrong. The Research page stores fair, buy-below and sell-above prices.
Internal Rate of Return — the money-weighted annual return that accounts for the timing and size of your buys/sells.
Time-Weighted Return — return that strips out the effect of deposits/withdrawals, for comparing to a benchmark.
Compound Annual Growth Rate — the constant yearly rate that turns the start value into the end value over the period.
Return after inflation (the app uses euro-area HICP). A 5% gain in a 3% inflation year is about 2% real.
Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices — the euro area's official inflation measure, used for real returns.
Euro Short-Term Rate — the ECB's overnight rate, used as the risk-free rate in Sharpe, Sortino and alpha.
Annualised standard deviation of returns: how widely the value swings. Not the same as the risk of permanent loss.
(Return − risk-free rate) / volatility: return earned per unit of total risk.
Like Sharpe but divides by downside volatility only, so upside swings are not penalised.
Annualised return / maximum drawdown.
How much the portfolio tends to move when the benchmark moves 1%. 1 = in line, below 1 = less sensitive.
Return above what beta and the benchmark explain, after the risk-free rate.
The largest peak-to-trough drop in portfolio value over the recorded history.
Herfindahl-Hirschman Index — a 0–10000 concentration score; lower means more diversified.
Trailing-12-month dividends from a position divided by what you paid for it.
Buying or selling to bring the portfolio back to its target allocation after markets have moved it.
Seeing a fund's underlying holdings (asset class, region, sector) instead of counting the fund as one opaque line.
Geometric Brownian Motion — the stochastic model the Wealth Simulator uses to project future value.
Running many random simulated futures to see the range of outcomes (e.g. the 10th–90th percentile band) rather than one projection.
ETF = exchange-traded fund, bought on an exchange like a share; index fund = a mutual fund that tracks an index (e.g. Indexa Capital holdings). Tracked as separate asset types.
Total Expense Ratio / Ongoing Charges Figure: the fund's yearly cost as a % of what you hold, taken out of the fund's value daily. Shown on the Analytics fees view.
How much all costs together lower your yearly return, e.g. 0.4% a year.
Net Asset Value — a fund's value per unit, calculated once a day; mutual funds are bought and sold at the NAV.
Accumulating (Acc) funds reinvest dividends inside the fund; distributing (Dist) funds pay them out (taxed in Spain when paid).
EU fund regulation. EU retail investors can generally only buy UCITS ETFs (often Irish or Luxembourg domiciled).
International Securities Identification Number — a 12-character code (e.g. IE00…) that identifies a security; the ticker can differ per exchange, the ISIN does not.
How closely a fund follows its index; the gap comes from costs, sampling and cash drag.
A fund share class that offsets currency moves (e.g. USD vs EUR) so you get the asset's local return, at a small cost.
An account where a provider chooses and rebalances the funds (e.g. Indexa Capital). The app tracks its holdings but never suggests trades in it.
UK pence — some London-listed prices are quoted in pence (÷100 for GBP).
Impuesto sobre la Renta de las Personas Físicas — Spanish personal income tax; investment income sits in the “savings base”.
The part of IRPF for investment income: gains, dividends, interest. Taxed in brackets of 19%–30% (2025 rates), separately from salary.
First-In, First-Out — the oldest shares are sold first when computing cost basis and realised gains (mandatory in Spain for identical securities).
A transfer between Spanish-registered mutual funds without selling: the gain is not taxed until you finally sell. Not available for ETFs or most stocks.
Art. 33.5 LIRPF: a loss on a sale cannot be declared if you buy the same security within 2 months before or after (1 year for unlisted fund units); it is deferred until those shares are sold.
Selling a position at a loss to offset gains realised in the same year. Losses not used can be carried forward four years.
Net savings-base losses that could not be offset in a year can offset gains in the following four years.
Tax withheld at source (19% in Spain on dividends and interest) and credited against your final IRPF bill. Foreign withholding can partly be credited too.
Information returns for assets held abroad over €50,000 (720: accounts, securities, property; 721: crypto held abroad).
Quarterly IRPF prepayment for the self-employed (autónomos); the cash-flow forecast can reserve for it.
Everything you own (investments, cash, property, other assets) minus everything you owe (mortgage, loans).
The share of income not spent in a month: (income − spending) / income.
Cash to cover several months of essential spending (often 3–6) without selling investments.
Financial Independence, Retire Early — a savings/investing target where assets cover your living costs.
The share of a portfolio you can spend each year with a low chance of running out (the classic '4% rule' comes from US data over 30 years).
The euro interbank rate that Spanish variable mortgages follow (usually 12-month Euribor + a spread).
TIN is the nominal interest rate; TAE (APR) is the effective yearly rate including compounding and fees, the one to compare offers with.
Paying down a loan's principal. In a French (annuity) mortgage early payments are mostly interest; an extra payment can shorten the term or lower the instalment.
Outstanding loan / property value. Lower LTV means more equity in the home.
The app's essentiality levels: fixed is contractual (mortgage, insurance), flexible can come down (groceries, energy), optional can stop (restaurants, subscriptions).
Portfolio Dividend Tracker — the spreadsheet format this app imports/exports and syncs with Google Sheets.

pages.title: Dashboard
pages.text: Your portfolio at a glance: total value, amount invested, cash, return and open positions. • Total value is your positions plus all idle cash. Invested is what you paid for the positions you hold, with what they're worth now on the line below. Both are in EUR. Foreign-currency holdings are converted at live FX rates. • Cash combines uninvested cash in your brokerage accounts (deposits/withdrawals/sells/dividends/interest not yet reinvested) with your bank account balances into one figure — included in Total value. See the Bank Accounts card for the per-account breakdown. • Return defaults to lifetime (cost-basis) return. Switching to YTD / 1Y uses daily snapshots, so it only covers the period since snapshots began. • The Risk, last 12 months row shows your return against the benchmark, how far you are below the 12-month high, volatility and Sharpe. Green / amber / red come with a word (Good, Pullback, Behind…); hover a label for the ranges. Volatility is described, not coloured — how much swing is acceptable depends on you. The same numbers, plus more, are on Analytics → Risk. • Top Positions and the allocation donut reflect current open positions by EUR value, plus a Cash slice. • The Goals card (shown once you have a goal) gives one line per goal: status, progress towards the target, time left, and the monthly amount needed against what you planned and your actual pace since the goal was set. Click a goal name to open the Goals page. • Customize (top right) lets you drag the blocks below the KPI tiles into your own order and hide the ones you don't use; the layout is saved on the server, so the phone and the desktop match. Reset layout brings the default back. • The Needs attention strip below the KPI tiles combines two groups: price signals (price targets crossed, watchlist buy zones, stale price data) and to-dos from the Action Items page (stale imports, data-quality issues, price-update errors, stale research, off-track goals, Net Worth setup). Click a group to expand it; the × hides it until something changes. • Hover any chart for exact values — the history chart shows value, cost basis and unrealised gain for each day; donuts show the amount and share of each slice. • Portfolio Value History plots actual daily snapshots (past) — cash isn't tracked historically, so it's positions-only, like the current value under Invested above. The Wealth Simulator card below it is a projection of the future, not history. Prices come from Yahoo Finance and are refreshed daily at 20:00 UTC.

pages.title: Analytics
pages.text: Seven tabs covering every angle of portfolio analysis. All values in EUR, prices from Yahoo Finance refreshed daily at 20:00 UTC. • Performance : total return (FIFO cost basis), money-weighted IRR, and period return vs a market benchmark over a selectable window (YTD / 1Y / 3Y / All). Period return needs daily snapshots. • Dividends : monthly bar chart of dividend income, trailing-12-month total, projected annual income, yield on cost per position, and an upcoming dividend calendar. • Gain / Loss : unrealised winners and losers leaderboard for your open positions, plus a year-by-year realised gains summary with a tax-report CSV export. • Tax : Spanish IRPF savings-base estimate — FIFO realised gains + dividends + interest taxed on the progressive 19/21/23/27/28% brackets. Also shows tax-loss harvesting candidates (open losses, with 2-month wash-sale flag). An estimate, not tax advice. • Risk : current and maximum drawdown, volatility, Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, beta and alpha over the last 12 months or all history — computed from flow-adjusted daily snapshot returns (needs at least 3 snapshots). Each rated metric shows a Good / OK / Weak label; hover it for the ranges. Under a year of history the ratings are greyed out as low confidence. • Risk also holds a Stress test card (preset shocks: loss, net worth before and after, retirement verdict). The Tax optimizer shows days left to 31 December, carry-forward losses and the tax each harvest would save. • Fees : total fees and withholding tax paid per broker, plus fee drag % of amount invested. • Diversification : sector, country, currency and asset-type breakdown with Herfindahl concentration index (HHI). Fetches fundamentals from Yahoo Finance — can be slow. Hover any metric label for its definition. Net Worth Over Time chart uses daily snapshots; history starts from the first recorded snapshot. Metrics Explained Return metrics • Total Return — total gain (price, sales, dividends, interest) ÷ everything you bought. Simple, not annualised. • IRR (money-weighted) — your return per year, including the effect of when you added money. Answers "how did my money do?" • TWR (time-weighted, Period Return) — strips out deposits and purchases. Answers "how did my investments do?" — the one to compare with a benchmark or a fund's published return. • Alpha — return beyond what market exposure (Beta) and the risk-free rate predict. All amounts are in EUR: what you paid at the exchange rate on the day you paid it, what you hold at today's rate — so currency gains and losses count as return. Benchmarks are converted to EUR the same way. Risk metrics • Volatility — annualised std dev of daily returns. Higher = bumpier ride. • Sharpe — return above the risk-free rate (€STR) per unit of total volatility. Penalises all swings equally. • Sortino — like Sharpe but only penalises swings below the risk-free rate. • Max Drawdown — worst peak-to-trough drop in the window. Current Drawdown — how far below the window's high you are now. • Calmar — annualised return ÷ worst drop. Combines return and worst-case loss in one number. • Beta — market sensitivity, from weekly returns. Not good or bad by itself; depends on your goals. Sources • Time- and money-weighted returns: CFA Institute, Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) 2020 . • Sharpe ratio: W. F. Sharpe, "The Sharpe Ratio", Journal of Portfolio Management , 1994. • Sortino ratio: F. Sortino & L. Price, "Performance Measurement in a Downside Risk Framework", Journal of Investing , 1994. • Calmar ratio: T. Young, "Calmar Ratio: A Smoother Tool", Futures , 1991. • Alpha: M. Jensen, "The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945–1964", Journal of Finance , 1968. • Risk-free rate: ECB, euro short-term rate (€STR), ECB Data Portal. • SRI risk classes: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/653 (PRIIPs KID), Annex II. The Good / OK / Weak bands for Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar and alpha are common rules of thumb, not official thresholds.

pages.title: Watchlist
pages.text: Securities you are considering but do not own yet. • Set a Buy below price; Distance to Buy shows how far the current price is from your target. • Prices are fetched live from Yahoo Finance when the page loads, so it may take a few seconds. This is a tracking aid, not a recommendation to buy.

pages.title: Reports
pages.text: Write-ups you saved from the AI Chat. A report is Markdown and can hold charts and tables, exactly as in the chat. • Save one answer with the bookmark button under it, or the whole thread with Export, Write report from this thread . • Pick a report on the left to read it. Charts can be downloaded or expanded and tables sorted or saved as CSV. • Rename , delete , download as Markdown or as a web page (charts embedded as images), or print it for a PDF.

pages.title: Loans & Mortgage
pages.text: One page for each loan you entered on Net Worth: where it stands, what is left to pay, whether the bank charges what the schedule says, and what an extra repayment would change. Add or edit loans on Net Worth; the only thing you change here is the rate history. • Cards. What you borrowed and how much of it is repaid, the balance today, rate (with the date it applies from), the monthly payment, the end date and the interest still to pay. Equity is the value of your property assets on Net Worth less the loan balance; with several loans the balance of all of them is used. • Amortisation. Balance at the end of each year, and how much of what you pay each year is principal and how much is interest. The yearly table is under the charts. If the loan has a recorded balance and rate date, the schedule starts there; add the rates it had before under Rate history and the earlier years appear dashed and lighter, marked history . Monthly payments below it lists every payment, past and future, by year: the payment, how much is principal and interest, and the balance after it; the next one is highlighted. • Rate history. The rates the loan had before its recorded balance (a first period from the loan start, then one per revision, optionally with the lender's balance on that date). Each period recalculates the payment over the remaining term. It adds what you paid so far, past years in the table, and compares the bank debits of those years with the rebuilt payment. The balance today, the end date and the interest still to pay do not change. • Payments vs bank. The scheduled payment against the debits in a bank category (the one named like the loan, else Mortgage ; type another to override). Differs means the bank charged another amount; two months in a row with the same difference usually means the rate was revised, so update the rate and balance on Net Worth. Not charged appears only when a statement reaches past the month; Pending means the statement does not cover the month yet. • What if I pay extra? A lump sum and/or an extra amount each month, used either to finish sooner (same payment) or to lower the payment (same end date). The optional investment comparison is a simple compound return before tax and costs. It is not advice. A rate change (a new rate, or a change in points, from a date) recalculates the payment over the payments that remain and shows the new payment and the interest difference; it is shown on its own, never combined with a repayment. • Detect from bank. On Net Worth, the loan form can fill itself from a recurring monthly debit in your bank rows (enter the principal and months to get the rate). Nothing is saved until you save the form.

pages.title: Decisions
pages.text: A journal for your investment decisions. Write one down when you make it, then look back when the time comes. • Record the decision with why you made it (rationale) and what you expect to happen. If you give a symbol we know, the latest stored price is saved with it. • Review on sets the date to look back. Once it passes the decision shows as due , and the Action Items page raises a reminder. • Review closes a decision: write what happened and rate it good, neutral, bad or unclear. Reopen clears the review. • Open decisions show the price then and now, so you can see how it moved since the day you decided. The point is to judge the reasoning, not only the result: a good decision can have a bad outcome and the other way round.

pages.title: Goals
pages.text: Set financial targets and check whether your current net worth plus monthly contributions keep you on track. • The strip at the top counts goals per status and adds up the monthly contributions your open goals assume — amber when that is more than your net monthly cash flow, because several goals can't each have the whole of it. • Each goal projects forward from your current net worth using your monthly contribution and an assumed annual return % (compounded). • Status: On track / Off track compare the projected value at the target date with the target; Achieved means your net worth is already past the target; Overdue means the date passed without reaching it. • Since set shows how your net worth has moved since the goal was created and the share of the gap that closed, and Pace compares the actual monthly change with what you planned and with what is still needed from now. It needs the goal's baseline (stored automatically for new goals; older goals get one via Edit → "Net worth when set"), and the first month shows no pace. Net worth includes market moves, so a bad month is not a missed deposit. • The button opens AI Chat with the goal's numbers filled in, so you can ask whether it is realistic and what to change. The chat can also read all goals itself ( get_goals ). • Goals also appear as a card on the Dashboard (one line each) and off-track or overdue goals as Action Items. • The "Monthly €" field is pre-filled with your current net Monthly Cash Flow (income − expenses, from the Net Worth page) when adding a new goal — still yours to edit, and different goals can assume different contributions. • Click the next to a goal's current/target figures to see the breakdown (brokerage + fixed deposits + manual assets − liabilities) behind the current net-worth number — useful when it's lower (or more negative) than you expect. Assumed returns are your inputs — actual results will vary.

pages.title: Wealth Simulator
pages.text: Projects your future net worth using a Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) model per asset class, plus deterministic mortgage amortization. Inputs • Stocks / ETFs value is auto-populated from your live holdings when the page loads. Hit the refresh icon to reload it. • Fill from my data fills the amounts from what pfm already knows: Cash = bank balances, cash lines and fixed deposits from the balance sheet; Stocks and Bonds = all investments (brokers, pensions, external accounts), split by the bond share after fund look-through; the mortgage balance, rate and payment from your loans (several loans are combined, the rate weighted by balance), or, with no loan entered, the balance from a manual Net Worth line in category Mortgage and the payment from Monthly Cash Flow (the rate is then left as it is); the Monthly contribution = average net savings over the last complete months of bank imports (or your Monthly Cash Flow entries when there are none). Each filled value says where it came from underneath. Returns, volatility, horizon and confidence are assumptions and are never touched. Property is not modelled. • Use my history sets the Stocks annual return from your money-weighted IRR since inception, minus 2% assumed inflation (the ECB's target) to make it a real return like the other inputs, and the volatility from the last 12 months of daily snapshots. • Annual return % per asset class is your assumed long-run real return, e.g. 8% for stocks, 4% for bonds, 1.5% for cash. • Volatility % (stocks only) controls how wide the confidence band is. Default 16%; your historical figure may differ. • Monthly contribution (under Stocks / ETFs) is added to the stocks bucket each month before compounding — it does not apply to cash or bonds. • Goals — tick any goal to overlay its target on the chart: a dashed line at the target amount, plus a marker at the target date if it falls within the years shown. A target far outside the chart's natural range (e.g. a much larger goal than the current projection) is shown as a small chip above the chart instead of a line, so it doesn't flatten everything else. Saved scenarios • Save stores the inputs under a name (e.g. "Base case", "Pay mortgage faster", "Retire at 60") together with a baseline : today's date and your balance-sheet net worth. The first scenario you save becomes the primary one (★), shown on the Dashboard and watched by Action Items; change it from a scenario's menu. • Load puts a scenario back into the inputs (the stocks value as saved — hit refresh for today's holdings). Update with current inputs overwrites it and restarts its tracking from today. • Tick the box next to scenarios to compare them: their expected paths are drawn as dashed lines on the chart and appear in the hover tooltip. • Plan vs actual (the card under the chart, for the loaded scenario) compares how your net worth has changed since the baseline with the change the scenario expected over the same days. On track means the real change lies inside the scenario's confidence band; Ahead / Behind means outside it. It works on changes, not levels, because the simulator models liquid assets minus the mortgage while the balance sheet also holds property and other manual lines. A verdict needs 30 days. Re-baseline restarts tracking from today without touching the inputs — use it when the plan itself changed (a big purchase, an inheritance). • Ask AI opens a chat thread with the scenario's inputs, expected outcome and tracking; the assistant can also read every saved scenario itself. Chart • The mean line is deterministic compound growth. The shaded band is the GBM confidence interval, widening over time as uncertainty compounds. • 50% likely range (default): half of the simulated outcomes fall inside the band. 95% : ~1 in 20 outcomes falls outside. 99% is wider but still not exhaustive — extreme events aren't modelled. Whatever the band, the y-axis stops at 2.5× the expected path so the expected line stays readable. • Net Worth = cash + stocks + bonds − remaining mortgage balance at each year. A statistical projection, not financial advice. See the Methodology panel on the page for the exact GBM formula.

pages.title: Transactions
pages.text: Your full transaction history — buys, sells and dividends across all brokers. • Filter by portfolio, type and date range. • Import from a broker file or pasted text (AI extraction), or add transactions manually. • Export everything as CSV or in Portfolio Dividend Tracker (PDT) XLSX format. Cost basis for tax and P/L uses FIFO from these records.

pages.title: Assets
pages.text: Your current open positions with cost basis, live price and profit/loss, plus the full catalogue of securities and funds you track — all in EUR. • Each asset has a symbol, type, exchange and currency. Assets are created automatically when you import transactions, or added manually here. • Avg Price is your FIFO cost basis; Current Price is the latest Yahoo Finance quote, refreshed daily at 20:00 UTC. • P/L is unrealised gain/loss on positions you still hold. Quantity, cost and P/L are blank for assets you don't currently hold — tick "Show assets with no holding" to include them in the table. • Research opens an LLM-generated fair-value analysis from fundamentals — informational, not advice. • Rebalancing compares your current allocation against your target percentages and suggests buys/sells to close the drift. Its Trade Plan section goes further: set constraints (cash budget, max trades, max sell gain, excluded/locked symbols) and generate an actual proposed trade list, shown as three strategies (tax-minimal, closest to target, balanced) covering all portfolios combined — planning output only, review before placing orders. Prices from Yahoo Finance, refreshed daily at 20:00 UTC; converted to EUR at live FX rates.

pages.title: Portfolios
pages.text: Broker and account groups used to organise your transactions. • Each import automatically creates a matching portfolio if one does not exist. • You can also create an account directly here with the Add Portfolio button — pick Brokerage for an investment account, or Bank to set up a checking/savings account for use with Spending tracking before importing anything. The account type can't be changed later, so choose carefully at creation time. • Filter transactions and analytics by portfolio elsewhere in the app.

pages.title: Import / Export
pages.text: Bring data in and out, manage cash bookings, back up your database and sync with Google Sheets. • File import supports IndexaCapital, MyInvestor, Mintos, Coinbase CSV and PDT XLSX; text import uses AI extraction for any broker statement. • Import Bank Statement lets you bring in a bank/checking account CSV from this page too — the same import flow as the Spending page, just accessible here alongside your other imports. • Bookings are cash deposits and withdrawals (no asset). • Backup : Download DB backup saves a full SQLite snapshot of your data. Restore DB backup replaces the live database from a .db or .db.gz file — a pre-restore snapshot is auto-saved if PFM_BACKUP_DIR is set. • Google Sheets sync pulls from / pushes to a spreadsheet in PDT format shared with the service account.

pages.title: Net Worth
pages.text: Your complete financial picture: brokerage investments plus off-brokerage assets and liabilities, all converted to EUR. History. A snapshot of the balance sheet is stored once a day. The History card draws net worth over time (or stacked by component) and What changed splits the move over the last month, 3 months or since the first snapshot into saved, market moves, debt paid down, property and other. History starts the day the first snapshot was stored. • Investments are auto-calculated from your portfolio positions. Fixed Deposits tracks active term deposits — only active ones count toward net worth, so click "Mark as Matured" once a deposit's term ends (this doesn't happen automatically) to record the interest and stop it inflating a stale total. • Add manual assets (cash, property, pension) and liabilities (mortgage, loans) to complete the picture. If you carry a mortgage, add your home's value too — otherwise the debt is counted with nothing offsetting it, which can make net worth look far more negative than reality. For a home's value, use a current market estimate (cadastral value or a comparable local listing), not the original purchase price — it's just a rough offset, not used for anything else. • For balances that change often (a bank account, say), click the € amount in the table to edit it in place — no need to delete and re-add. Bank/cash rows show when they were last updated, flagged in amber past 30 days. • The Setup checklist card flags common gaps — home value, bank accounts, income, mortgage/loan payments, other recurring expenses — and overdue-but-still-active deposits; the "Run setup wizard" button walks through filling them in one at a time. • Monthly Cash Flow tracks rough recurring income (salary, other) vs expenses (mortgage payment, loan, rest) for your own reference — it does not currently feed Goals or Forecast projections. • FIRE goals project from total net worth, not just the brokerage value. • If you import bank statements on the Spending page, an "Actual" comparison appears here for the last 30 days — read-only, doesn't change the manual figures above. All amounts converted to EUR at live FX rates.

pages.title: Budget
pages.text: What you planned to earn, spend, invest and repay each month, compared against what actually happened. Everything on the actual side is data the app already holds — imported bank statements and broker deposits — so a budget needs no separate bookkeeping. Month close. The Month close tab walks through a finished month: imports, uncategorised rows, transfers, unusual charges and missing recurring charges, then the month's figures. Close saves them with a report; Reopen removes the mark. • Budgets are open-ended. A line's monthly amount applies to every month you look at; you edit it in place as life changes rather than rebuilding it each January. For costs that land in one month (insurance, holidays), use the per-month override editor on that line instead of smearing the cost across the year. • Start with "Seed from actuals" on the Edit tab. It reads your last 12 complete months and proposes a line per top-level category with a suggested amount — review, adjust, apply. Nothing is written until you click Apply. • Four kinds of line. Spending and Income match against categorized bank rows; Debt is a spending category tracked separately so mortgage/loan repayments don't hide inside general spending; Investment matches deposits into a broker account. • One line per branch. You can budget a group ("Housing") or its children ("Rent", "Utilities"), but not both — a parent's actual already includes its children, so both lines would count the same euros. The app blocks the overlap and names the conflicting line. • "Not budgeted" rows show real spending in categories with no line, and they count toward the actual total. Without them, "under budget" could just mean most of your spending isn't in the plan. • Variance is signed so positive is good — under plan on a cost, above plan on income or a contribution. Green is favourable regardless of which way round the line reads. • Pace. For the month in progress each cost line shows where it is heading by month end ( On track , At risk , Over ): spent so far, plus recurring charges still to come, plus the line's usual everyday spending for the rest of the month, measured to the date your least up-to-date account's statement runs to. Too early means there is no baseline yet and little of the month has passed. A month with nothing imported shows no pace. Irregular marks a line spent in only a few months of the last year ("irregular: spent in 2 of 12 months"): its pace is what is already spent plus recurring charges still due, with no everyday average. • Planned items and what-if (Forecast tab). Add known future expenses or income and they are placed on their dates in the forecast, next to an estimated quarterly tax. The what-if row tries one extra amount without saving it. • Seeding now suggests, per category, whether to plan it monthly, yearly or monthly with carry-over, with the reason; you can switch each, and an existing line can be converted to yearly or given carry-over. • Yearly lines and carry over. Spending and debt lines can be yearly (enter the yearly figure; a twelfth is the cash to set aside each month, and the line is over only when the last 12 months of spending exceed the yearly figure) or carry what is left over from month to month within the calendar year. Variance is then against what is available. • Forecast tab. Where this month ends and the next 12 months, with the projected bank balance, the bills known to be coming, how fresh each account's data is and the assumptions. It works without a budget. • Scenarios. Create several budgets (base, best case, worst case) and duplicate one into another as a starting point. Exactly one is active : that's the one the Dashboard card and Action Items use. Amounts are converted to EUR at today's rate and exclude transfers between your own accounts — the same conventions as the Spending page, so the two reconcile. Actual figures come from the Spending page's imports, so a month with no statement imported will read as under budget.

pages.title: Spending
pages.text: Categorized day-to-day spending imported from your bank/checking accounts — separate from the investment transactions tracked elsewhere in the app. • Import a statement (CSV: date, description, amount) via the button top-right, or from the Import Bank Statement card on the Import/Export page — both open the same import flow. If any imported rows look like duplicates of what's already saved, a Skip / Add anyway / Overwrite existing selector appears so you decide how to handle them before saving. Each row is matched against your saved category rules (a keyword in the description, e.g. "MERCADONA" → Groceries); anything left uncategorized can be resolved with the "Suggest categories (AI)" button — review and edit before saving. Accepting a suggestion creates a new rule automatically, so future imports for that merchant auto-categorize. • Transfers between your own accounts (e.g. checking → savings, or checking → a brokerage account already tracked here) are detected automatically by matching an outflow in one account to an inflow of the same amount within a few days in another — shown separately, not counted as spending. Use "Re-scan transfers" if you import a matching account's statement later. • Select one or more rows with the checkbox column to bulk recategorize or delete them via the action bar that appears above the table — there's no single-row delete button, so even one row needs to be checked first. • Search matches the bank's description and the cleaned-up merchant name (card numbers, towns and reference codes stripped). • Click a category in the table to change it by hand at any time. If other uncategorized rows share the merchant, you're offered a rule that files them all. • Rules can be limited to one account, money in or out, and an amount range. Lower priority numbers are tried first. • Recurring lists charges that arrive at a steady interval for a steady amount. Missed means a statement covering the due date is imported but the charge isn't in it. The ... menu on a row marks it Cancelled (leaves the yearly total and the forecast; counted as savings) or Paid another way (still in the yearly total, out of the forecast); Came back means it charged again after you marked it. Switch the order to By yearly cost to review subscriptions dearest first. • When a statement has a balance column, the import preview warns if the balances don't add up, which usually means missing rows. • One-off. Flag a payment as one-off (the flag button on a row, or the bulk bar) when it will not repeat. It still counts in your totals but is left out of averages, comparisons and the forecast. • Analytics also compares a month with your normal and with last year, flags unusual charges (mark one-off or dismiss) and splits spending into fixed, flexible and optional by month. • To classify (top of Transactions) groups uncategorized rows by merchant, biggest money first: pick a category, optionally add a rule, and the whole group is filed in one step. Analytics also has a Year card comparing a year with the one before, like for like. • Essentiality (Categories tab, spending categories only) says how hard a category is to cut: Fixed is contractual and hard to change within months (mortgage, insurance, school), Flexible is needed but the amount can come down (groceries, energy, transport), Optional can stop (restaurants, subscriptions, travel). Suggest with AI proposes a level for each category that has none; nothing is saved until you accept. The AI Chat uses these levels to answer "what should I cut first?". A read-only summary of the last 30 days also appears on the Net Worth page, next to your manual Monthly Cash Flow entries, for comparison.

pages.title: Your progress
pages.text: Numbers for a long-term investor: where your money came from, how each year went after inflation, what tax would take, and whether your saving habit and cash buffer are in place. • Market growth — value minus the money you put in (purchases minus sale proceeds). Early on most of a portfolio is your own savings; with time, growth should take over. • Real return — your yearly return (IRR) after Spanish inflation. If it's above zero, your money buys more than it did. • Year by year — time-weighted return per calendar year, the way funds report theirs, next to the benchmark in EUR and inflation. Bad years are normal: the MSCI World index fell about 18% in US dollars in 2022 (about 13% in euros). • If you sold everything today — the IRPF savings-base tax (19–28%) your unrealised gains would add this year. Funds can be switched with a traspaso without paying it; ETFs and shares can't. • Savings rate — share of income not spent, from imported bank statements. • Emergency fund — months of spending your bank cash covers. Build this before investing more. Sources • Time-weighted and money-weighted returns: CFA Institute, GIPS 2020 . • Inflation: HICP Spain, Eurostat (via the ECB Data Portal). • Savings tax: Ley 35/2006 del IRPF (base del ahorro; art. 49 for offsetting losses against dividends and interest). • Savings-rate band: the 50/30/20 rule (E. Warren & A. Warren Tyagi, All Your Worth , 2005). The coloured bands are rules of thumb, not official thresholds. Not tax or investment advice.

pages.title: Stress Testing — Methodology
pages.text: Stress testing answers: "If a historical crash happened today, how much would my current portfolio lose at the worst point?" For each open position the tool fetches the asset's actual historical return over the scenario window from Yahoo Finance, then applies that percentage to the current EUR value. Assets without a matching Yahoo symbol use an asset-class average (marked * ). Preset scenarios Scenario Window Duration What happened 2008 Crisis Oct 2007 → Mar 2009 ~17 months Global banking collapse; S&P 500 −57% 2020 COVID 19 Feb → 23 Mar 2020 33 days Pandemic panic selling; S&P 500 −34% 2022 Rates 31 Dec 2021 → 12 Oct 2022 ~9.5 months Aggressive rate hikes; S&P 500 −25%, bonds −15% Dot-com 24 Mar 2000 → 9 Oct 2002 ~2.5 years Tech bubble burst; Nasdaq −78% Asset-class fallback rates (used when no Yahoo data is available) Asset type 2008 2020 2022 Dot-com Stock / ETF / Index −50% −32% −22% −60% Mutual fund −40% −25% −18% −45% Bond −5% +5% −15% +5% Crypto 0% −50% −65% 0% Commodity −30% −20% +20% −15% Cash 0% 0% 0% 0% Crypto fallback is 0% for 2008 and dot-com because Bitcoin did not exist (no data, not because it was unaffected). Custom date range Enter any start and end date to replay that window against your current holdings. Custom runs are not cached — each click fetches live data from Yahoo Finance. The S&P 500 return over that window is used as the equity fallback for assets without historical data. Limitations • Snapshot, not simulation. The result is the loss at the crash bottom. It does not model the recovery, nor any action you might have taken (rebalancing, stop-losses, new contributions). • Dividends ignored. Income received during the crash window is not counted. • Today's holdings, not historical ones. The tool applies past returns to your current positions — it does not reconstruct what you actually held during that period. • Preset results cached 7 days. The four named scenarios are cached in the database; custom ranges always run live. • FX effects not modelled. All EUR conversions use current FX rates, not crisis-era rates. Informational only, not financial advice.

pages.title: Research
pages.text: Deep-dive on any ticker: fundamentals, your position, a thesis, and an LLM valuation backed by live news. Portfolio Health Click Run Analysis to get a scored health report across five dimensions (Diversification, Risk/Return, Income, Fees, Tax Efficiency), each rated 1–10 with an explanation and a prioritised action list. Results are cached — adjust the cache duration in Settings → Portfolio Advisor. Workbench • Search any symbol → see Yahoo Finance fundamentals (P/E, yield, sector), your cost basis and P/L, set fair/buy/sell prices, write a thesis and get an AI analysis with news citations. • Under the targets, a muted line shows the calibrated fair value (the stored fair value shrunk by how your past reports scored) and the headroom left under the symbol's position cap . The Scorecard tab has the calibration table. • Save a research note to version your thinking over time. Saved price targets are pushed to your alerts so you get notified when a price is crossed. Compare Shows the latest saved note per symbol with current price vs fair value and upside %. LLM analysis is informational, not financial advice. Fundamentals from Yahoo Finance.

pages.title: Diagnostics
pages.text: Three tabs: Price Health monitors live price data; Data Quality runs automated checks on your transaction records; Logs shows warnings, errors and every LLM call. The overview chips above the tabs summarise all three, and each tab shows a count of what is still open. Following up. Every Data Quality finding can be marked checked (looked at, fine — add a note saying why) or snoozed for a while. The state is stored on the server, so your phone, your laptop and the AI chat all see the same list, and the Action Items page only counts findings nobody has checked. A finding id names one concrete occurrence, so a new duplicate never hides behind an old check. Discuss with AI opens a chat thread with today's freshness, last run and open findings as context; the chat can also read them itself ( get_diagnostics ) and record your decision ( set_action_item_status ). Price Health tab • Freshness : hours since the last price refresh. Fresh = under 30 h; Aging = 30–48 h or one or more stale holdings; Very stale = over 48 h. • Stale & unpriced holdings : auto-priced assets whose latest stored price is older than 4 days, or that have never been priced. Assets with auto-price disabled (manual prices) are excluded. • Update history : each daily run (20:00 UTC) logs duration, updated/skipped/error counts, the symbols that failed (with the API error) and the ones skipped. Data Quality tab Cash & Position Reconciliation For each portfolio, computes: Implied Cash = Deposits − Withdrawals − Buy costs + Sell proceeds + Dividends + Interest Invested Value = held shares × latest stored price (EUR). Total Accounted = Implied Cash + Invested Value. Compare Implied Cash against your broker's actual cash balance to spot missing transactions. Possible Duplicate Transactions Groups transactions by portfolio / asset / type, then flags pairs where: • LIKELY (red): same calendar date and quantity within ±1% and price within ±1%. • POSSIBLE (yellow): dates within ±3 days and quantity within ±5% and price within ±5%. Use Delete older to remove the earlier of the two, or pick a specific row from the dropdown. Mark findings that are intentional (e.g. two separate partial fills on the same day) as checked , with a note. Suspicious Patterns Five automated checks run chronologically across all transactions: • zero_price (warning): a buy or sell recorded with price = 0 (splits and dividends are exempt). • zero_qty (warning): a buy or sell with quantity = 0. • negative_position (warning): a sell that would push the running held quantity below zero — usually a missing buy. • dividend_before_buy (info): a dividend recorded before the first buy for that asset — may indicate an import ordering issue. • price_outlier (warning): a buy/sell price that is more than 5× or less than 0.2× the median price for that asset (requires at least 3 price data points). Common cause: GBX/GBP unit confusion. Checked and snoozed findings are stored on the server (shared by every device and the AI chat); "Show checked" at the foot of a card lists them again, and a finding can be reopened at any time.

pages.title: Action Items
pages.text: A single checklist of everything that needs your attention across the app — pulled from Diagnostics, Net Worth, Goals, Watchlist, Budget, Spending, Allocation and Research so you don't have to visit each page separately. Following up. Checked means you looked at it and it is fine (add a note saying why); Snooze hides it for a week or a month. Both are stored on the server, shared by every device and the AI chat. Filter by severity, and switch on Show checked & snoozed to review or reopen earlier decisions. Ask AI on an item opens a chat thread about that one finding; the button in the header does it for every open item. In the chat you can also say "mark that as checked" — the assistant records it with set_action_item_status . Groups. Three or more similar open items (every price target crossed, budget lines on pace to exceed their limit, several stale imports) are folded into one row with a count. Open it with Show to see the items; each keeps its own Checked and Snooze. Checked or Snooze on the group row applies to every item in it at once. The list is sorted by priority: severity first, then what costs money or has a deadline, then routine housekeeping. • Broker Imports : a broker/portfolio with transaction history but no activity in 60+ days. • Data Quality : possible duplicate transactions or suspicious patterns (same checks as the Diagnostics Data Quality tab). • Errors : the most recent price-update run had failures, or held positions haven't been re-valued in 90+ days. • Goals : a savings goal is projected to miss its target. • Price Alerts : a watchlist symbol dropped into its buy zone, or a held position crossed a saved price target. • Net Worth : setup gaps (missing bank balance, income, etc.) or a fixed deposit past maturity — same checklist as the Net Worth page. • Budget / Spending / Allocation / Fund Exposure / Retirement : overruns, missed recurring charges, idle cash, funds without a look-through profile, a retirement plan that falls short. Item ids name one concrete occurrence, so checking an item hides it only until the underlying issue changes (e.g. a new failing price-update run gets its own item). Data Quality items count only the findings nobody has checked on the Diagnostics page.

pages.title: Chat
pages.text: Ask questions about your portfolio in natural language, or paste a broker statement to extract transactions. • Answers are generated by an LLM using your portfolio data — informational, not financial advice. • Shift+Enter (or Ctrl+Enter) sends; Enter adds a new line. • The model picker chooses the tier for the next answer: fast is cheap and quick, heavy reasons the most. Each answer shows the model that wrote it. • Used N tools under an answer opens the data lookups the model made (tool, arguments, time) — if it isn't there, the answer came from the summary context only. • A new thread is named automatically after its first answer; rename it from the thread list at any time. • Export saves the thread as Markdown or a web page (charts embedded as images), or opens the print dialog for a PDF. Write report from this thread asks the assistant for a structured report (up to a minute) and opens it on the Reports page. • Charts have a download (PNG) and an expand button; click a bar, slice or point to ask for that item in more detail. Tables have a CSV button and sort when you click a header. • Under the latest answer, follow-up chips send a suggested next question, and Sources lists the web pages used. The bookmark button under an answer saves it as a report. • Web search (shown when the server offers it) lets the assistant look things up online. Searches leave this machine; your personal figures are not included in the queries. • Extract pulls buy/sell transactions out of pasted text for you to review before saving. • Questions about the app itself ("how do I import from Coinbase?") or a term ("what is capex?") are answered from this Help and its glossary (tool get_app_help ). The box at the bottom of the Help page opens such a thread here.

metrics.text: Loan-to-value: the loan balance as a share of the value of your property assets on Net Worth. Lower is safer; the property value is only as fresh as its 'as of' date.
Property value less the loan balance. Only as good as the property value you entered.
Principal and interest paid since the loan started, rebuilt from the rate history plus the schedule from the recorded balance. Only shown when the history makes it complete.
The rates the loan had before its recorded balance. Each one recalculates the payment over the remaining term. The first covers any time before it.
The loan's original amount, and how much of it is paid off: the amount borrowed less the balance today.
Interest still to pay until the last scheduled payment, if the rate stays as entered.

Money-Weighted IRR: the yearly interest rate that makes all your purchases, sales, dividends and today's value balance out — the return you earned on your money, including the effect of when you added it. Source: CFA Institute, GIPS 2020 (money-weighted return).

Total Return: total gain (price changes on what you hold, gains on what you sold, dividends and interest) divided by everything you've spent on purchases, all in EUR at the rates on the day. Lifetime, not annualised.

Total Gain: unrealised gain on what you hold + realised gain on what you sold + dividends and interest received, in EUR. Costs paid on trades are already inside the purchase and sale amounts; ongoing fund fees are inside the fund's price.

Time-weighted return per year since your first trade: daily returns chained with deposits and purchases taken out, so it measures the investments rather than when you added money. This is the figure to compare with a benchmark or a fund's published return. Source: CFA Institute, GIPS 2020.
Period Return: time-weighted return over the selected window from daily snapshots — purchases and sales don't count as gains or losses. Source: CFA Institute, GIPS 2020.

What drove the return: each position's gain in the window = value at the end − value at the start − purchases + sales + dividends and interest, so money you add is never counted as a gain. The return is a simple Dietz: gain divided by the start value plus half the net money invested. A * marks a position valued at cost at a boundary because no price was stored.

My own accounts: text that identifies you or your own standing orders in a bank description, so a payment to an account you did not import is still treated as a move between your accounts rather than spending. Put here: your own name as the bank prints it, labels of your own standing orders. Do not put here: a partner's name, a generic bank word such as 'transfer' or 'transferencia', or a tax id that also appears on tax payments, because every row containing it would be marked. Removing an entry does not unmark rows already marked.

Position caps: the most a symbol, a sector or an asset type may weigh in the portfolio, as a % of total value. Headroom is how much more you could add before the cap (negative = over it). Near = less than 2 percentage points of headroom, breached = over it. A 'default stock cap' row is the allocator's built-in limit for a stock without its own cap. The Next-euro allocator respects these caps.

Stress test: applies a preset shock to today's holdings (funds are looked through into equity, bond and sector slices) and shows the loss, the net worth before and after, and the retirement verdict recomputed with the smaller pot. Funds without a profile are assumed to be all equity. It is a what-if on current values, not a forecast.

Year-end tax planning: days left until 31 December to realise losses. Carry-forward losses from the previous four years offset gains first. 'Tax saved' per candidate is the marginal IRPF saving of selling that position at a loss. A position bought in the last 2 months (or 1 year for unlisted funds) cannot be harvested: the loss is disallowed.

Calibrated fair value: your past research reports are scored against what the price did. The shrink factor is realised return divided by implied return (0.1 to 1.0); the calibrated fair value moves the stored fair value that fraction of the way from today's price. Hit rate is how often the direction was right. Based on the report's confidence bucket when it has at least 5 scored reports, else all reports. Small samples say little.

Research scorecard: each stored report is checked against what the price did afterwards, at two points. 'At horizon' is the report's own horizon (default 12 months) after it was written. 'At next report' is the date the next report for the same symbol was written. Direction hit: BUY needs a rise, SELL a fall, HOLD a move within 10%. Target error is (price - fair value) / fair value. Reached target: the price touched the fair value at some point in between. Reports still before their horizon are pending and show the return so far. Manual notes with a fair value count too. Small samples say little.
Herfindahl Index (HHI): concentration score 0–10000. Above 2500 = concentrated, below 1500 = well diversified.

Sharpe Ratio: yearly return above the risk-free rate (the euro overnight rate, €STR), divided by volatility — how much extra return each unit of swing earned. The bands are a common rule of thumb, not an official scale. Source: W. F. Sharpe, 'The Sharpe Ratio', Journal of Portfolio Management, 1994.
Inception Date: date of your first transaction — where lifetime returns start.

Sortino Ratio: like Sharpe, but the denominator only counts swings below the risk-free rate (the downside deviation), so upside jumps aren't treated as risk. The bands are a rule of thumb. Source: F. Sortino & L. Price, 'Performance Measurement in a Downside Risk Framework', Journal of Investing, 1994.

Calmar Ratio: annualised return ÷ the size of the worst drop. Above 1 means a typical year earns more than the worst fall cost. The original definition uses 36 months; here it uses the selected window, so treat a 1-year figure as indicative. Source: T. Young, 'Calmar Ratio: A Smoother Tool', Futures, 1991.

Beta: how much the portfolio tends to move when the benchmark moves, both in EUR. 1.0 = moves with it; above 1 swings more; below 1 swings less. Measured on weekly returns, because daily returns of markets that close at different hours don't line up.

Alpha: yearly return above what the portfolio's beta and the benchmark would predict, after the risk-free rate (Jensen's alpha). Positive = beat the market-risk-adjusted expectation. Source: M. Jensen, Journal of Finance, 1968.

Volatility: annualised standard deviation of daily returns — how much the portfolio value swings. The SRI class is the EU's 1–7 risk scale printed on every fund's key information document (KID), by volatility band; the official class uses 5 years of returns, so this is an indication. Source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/653, Annex II.
Max Drawdown: largest peak-to-trough drop over the window, measured on returns (buys and sells don't count as rises or drops).
Current Drawdown: how far the portfolio sits below its highest point in the window, measured on returns (buys and sells don't count).
Return vs benchmark: your time-weighted return over the window minus the benchmark's return over the same days, in percentage points.
All risk metrics use flow-adjusted (time-weighted) daily returns: money you put in or take out, and trades imported later, are not counted as gains or losses.
Fair Value: an estimate of intrinsic worth from fundamentals + an LLM analyst. Compare to current price.
Yield on Cost: trailing-12-month dividends from a position divided by what you paid for it.
Fee Drag: total fees paid as a percentage of the amount invested — how much costs eat your capital.

Ongoing charges (TER): the fund's yearly running cost as a percentage of its value, the 'ongoing charges' figure on the UCITS key investor document (KIID). It is taken out of the fund's price, so it never appears as a transaction. Set it per fund in the fund profile; funds without one are left out of the average.

Reduction in yield (RIY): how many percentage points per year the charges take off the return over the horizon, the way the EU PRIIPs key information document shows costs (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/653). Here it covers ongoing charges only, on an assumed gross return of 5% a year - an assumption for comparison, not a forecast.

Market growth: current value minus the money you put in (purchases minus sale proceeds), as a share of that money. Early on most of a portfolio is your own savings; over decades growth should take over. Dividends and interest paid out to cash are shown separately.

Real return: your money-weighted return per year (IRR) after Spanish inflation, using (1 + IRR) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. This is the growth in what your money can buy — what matters for a pension 20 years out. Inflation: HICP Spain (Eurostat, via the ECB). The bands are a rule of thumb.

Source: where this number comes from. Positions are your tracked holdings at the latest price; Broker cash is the cash ledger of a broker; Account API is the value an account reports itself (Indexa); Bank statement is the balance on your latest imported statement; Deposit is a fixed deposit principal; Loan schedule is the balance computed from the loan's terms; Manual is a figure you typed in.

Stale: this figure is older than its freshness limit (positions 4 days, account API 7, bank statement 45, broker cash 60, cash and bank accounts typed by hand 90, property 365, other manual items 180). It is still counted; update it to trust the total.
Financial assets: cash + fixed deposits + investments. Property and other assets are excluded. This is the pot a retirement plan can draw on, since a home you live in does not pay for groceries.

Retirement verdict: On track means the money lasts to your planning horizon age in the base case. Short means it runs out, but more than ten years after you stop working. At risk means it runs out sooner. The pessimistic line repeats the test with a lower real return.
Deployable: liquid cash minus the tax reserve (IVA and IRPF still owed on work income) minus the emergency buffer target. Only this part is proposed for investing.

Emergency buffer: liquid cash measured in months of your average monthly spending. Below the minimum it is rebuilt first; between minimum and target it is topped up; above the maximum the excess is idle cash.
Tax reserve: IVA and IRPF accrued on work income for quarters that are not yet paid, kept out of the deployable amount.
Reasons: why each line was chosen (bucket gap to target, cheapest fund, portfolio, caps). The runner-up is the next-best option and why it lost.

Sustainable spend: the constant total monthly spend, in today's euros, that your pot and your pensions together can fund from retirement to the horizon age (pensions are included in the figure). The gap is your spending target minus this figure; a negative gap is a surplus.
Save more: the extra amount you would need to put aside every month from today until retirement for the money to last to the horizon age. If no amount of saving is enough, the card says so.
Before tax: the screen does not model tax on withdrawals beyond the single withdrawal tax percentage in the plan settings (0 by default), so real spending power will be lower.

Emergency fund: cash in your bank accounts (and cash entered on Net Worth) divided by your average monthly spending over the last imported months. The usual guideline is 3–6 months; with freelance income, aim for the top of that range before investing more. A rule of thumb, not an official threshold.

Savings rate: (income − spending) ÷ income over the last 12 complete months that have imported bank statements, transfers between your own accounts left out. 20% is the savings share of the 50/30/20 rule (E. Warren & A. Warren Tyagi, All Your Worth, 2005). A rule of thumb.

Year by year: the time-weighted return of each calendar year (CFA Institute, GIPS 2020), next to the benchmark in EUR and Spanish inflation over the same months. 'part' marks a year that started late or is still running.

If you sold everything today: the extra IRPF savings-base tax this year (19–28%) on your unrealised gains, on top of what this year's sales and dividends already owe; net losses would lower it. Fund gains can be moved to another fund by traspaso without paying tax. Average-cost estimate, not tax advice.

Benchmark: a market index measured in EUR over the same days. Choose one with dividends reinvested (an accumulating ETF such as VWCE or IWDA): a price-only index like the S&P 500 leaves out about 1.5–2%/yr of dividends, which flatters the comparison.
Net Worth: total portfolio value in EUR (all currencies converted at current FX rates).
Invested: cost basis of your currently-held positions (what you paid, in EUR).

Savings Base (base del ahorro): the Spanish IRPF income category for investment income — realised capital gains plus dividends. Taxed on a progressive scale (19/21/23/27/28%), separate from your salary.
Realised Gain/Loss: profit or loss actually locked in by selling, using FIFO cost basis. Only realised gains are taxed.
Unrealised Gain/Loss: paper profit on positions you still hold (current value − cost basis). Not taxed until you sell.
Estimated Tax: progressive IRPF savings-base brackets applied to this year's realised gains + dividends. An estimate, not tax advice.
Tax-Loss Harvesting: positions currently at an unrealised loss. Selling them would realise a loss that offsets taxable gains (watch the 2-month wash-sale rule).
Snapshots: a daily record of your portfolio's total value and cost, saved by the price cron. Risk and period-return charts are built from these, so history starts when snapshots began.

Diversification: your holdings grouped by asset class, region, sector, country, currency and asset type. Direct holdings use Yahoo Finance fundamentals; fund and ETF positions are looked through using each fund's stored profile (benchmark index weights, or entered by hand) since Yahoo Finance has no geography for funds. Concentration (HHI) measures how lopsided the mix is.
P/L (Profit & Loss): current value minus cost basis, in euros. Unrealised while you still hold the position.
P/L % (Profit & Loss): current value minus cost basis, as a percentage of cost basis.
Planned: what the selected budget says you intended for the period — each line's monthly amount, plus any per-month overrides.
Actual: what really happened, from imported bank statements (spending and income) and broker deposits (contributions), excluding transfers between your own accounts.
Variance: planned minus actual, signed so positive is always the good direction — under budget on a cost, above plan on income or a contribution.
Not budgeted: real spending in categories your budget has no line for. Counted in the actual total, so "under budget" can't be an artifact of leaving half your spending out of the plan.

Month vs normal: one month's spending per category (or merchant) against the average of up to the 6 complete months before it that have imported statements, and against the same month a year earlier. Rows marked one-off still count in the month's actual but are left out of the normal. Only a complete month is compared: a month in progress, a month the imported data stops short of, or a month with nothing imported shows no deltas, because comparing part of a month with a full average would flatter it. Money moved to Invest or House purchase is shown apart, not as spending.

Unusual charges: a charge far above what that merchant usually bills, a large first charge from a new merchant, a category whose complete-month total is well above its normal, or the same merchant and amount twice within a few days. Deterministic rules, no AI. 'Mark one-off' keeps the row in your totals but stops it counting as normal; 'Dismiss' records it as checked (the same follow-up state as Action Items).

Fixed, flexible, optional: monthly spending split by the essentiality you set on each category (Categories tab). A category with no level, and none inherited from its parent, stays 'unclassified' rather than guessed. Money moved to Invest or House purchase is not spending and is left out. Months with no imported statement show no bar, not a zero.

One-off: a single unusual payment (a repair, a trip, an annual bill) you do not expect to repeat. It still counts in every total and in the budget's actuals, but it is left out of averages and baselines: the comparison's normal, anomaly detection, budget seeding and the cash-flow forecast.

Planned: one-off expenses, savings or income you know are coming (a trip, a repair, a bonus). Each is placed once, on its date, in the forecast and never enters an average. Overdue means its date is before the date your bank data runs to: mark it done (it is now in your statements) or move the date, otherwise it is not projected. Done items stay in the list but leave the forecast.

What if: add one unsaved amount in a month and see the lowest projected balance with and without it, the month it happens and whether it takes the balance below zero. Nothing is saved; press Clear to go back. If the forecast has no starting balance the answer reads 'not available'.

Estimated quarterly tax: the IVA and IRPF still to pay, worked out from your work income with the percentages in Settings > Allocator. 'Accrued so far' is what the quarter has built up; 'Average of past quarters' is used for quarters that have not started. It is an estimate for planning cash, not a tax return, and it needs the work-income merchants to be ticked in the allocator settings.

To classify: bank rows with no category, grouped by merchant with the biggest money first. Pick a category and Apply files the whole group in one step; tick 'Also add a rule' (and edit the text to match) so the next import files it by itself. Transfers are not listed, and a category must fit the direction of the money (a Spend category for money out).

Year against last year, like for like: only months that are complete and have imported statements in both years are added up, on both sides. For a year in progress the previous year is cut to the same months and its full total is shown next to it. A month with no imports is unknown, not zero. One-off payments count in the totals and are listed apart; money moved to Invest or House purchase is shown as saved, not spent.

Net worth: the latest stored balance sheet (investments, cash, property and other assets, less debts) and how it moved, split into what you saved, market moves and debt paid down. One snapshot is stored a day; the history starts at the first snapshot and is not backfilled.

Cash-flow outlook: your bank balance at the latest import, the projected balance at month end and the lowest month-end balance over the next three months, plus the next known bills. An estimate from past averages and recurring charges; it covers bank accounts only, not brokers.

Upcoming: what is dated in the next 30 days, in one list: recurring bills on their expected dates, your planned items, the estimated quarterly tax and journal decisions due for review. Bills start at the latest bank import, because a charge after that date has not been seen yet. Amounts are estimates from past charges.

Month close: where last month's close stands. The checks that still need a look are listed; the figures are that month's income, spending, savings and net. Closing is a mark, not a lock, and is done on the Budget page.
Loans: what you still owe on each loan, the share of the original amount repaid, the monthly payment and the end date, from the loan details you entered on the Net Worth page.

Subscriptions: recurring charges detected in your bank statements, with what they cost per month and per year and the most expensive ones. A series you marked cancelled or paid elsewhere is left out. 'Missed' means a charge was due and no statement shows it.

Latest movers: the positions whose latest price change moved your portfolio most, in euros, measured between each asset's last two stored prices. That is one day for most assets and longer over a weekend. Positions with a single or an old price are left out.

This week: the few most important open Action Items, most pressing first. Severity comes first, then what costs money or has a deadline, then routine housekeeping. A family of three or more similar items (for example every price target crossed) is one line with a count; open the Action Items page to see and check them one by one.

History: one stored snapshot of your balance sheet a day, taken after each price update or when you press Snapshot now. It starts the day the first snapshot was stored; nothing before that is reconstructed, because a rebuilt past would be a guess. Components shows the same snapshots split into investments, cash, property and other assets, with liabilities below zero.

What changed: the net-worth change between two stored snapshots, split into what you saved (the change in cash plus what you put into investments), market moves on the investments, debt you paid down, property and other. The parts add up to the change. A part that cannot be worked out says not available instead of a number. The start snaps to the nearest stored snapshot; a window longer than your history is not shown.

Month close: a checklist for the end of a month and a mark that says it is done. Imports is the only step that blocks: every bank account with recent rows must reach the last day of the month (Close anyway overrides it). The other steps are reminders: uncategorised outflows, transfers not yet linked, unusual charges, recurring charges that did not arrive, and big new one-off payments. Closing saves the figures and a Markdown report under Reports. It is a mark, not a lock: if rows change later, the page says the figures have changed, and you can close again. Reopen removes the mark and keeps the report.

Mark a recurring charge as Cancelled (you ended it: it leaves the yearly total, the forecast and the budget pace, and the cancellations are counted as savings) or Paid another way (you still pay it, but not from this account: it stays in the yearly total, and leaves the forecast and the pace). If it charges this account again, it shows Came back and counts as active until you mark it again or clear the mark.

Pace: for the month in progress, where a cost line is heading by month end. Projected month end = spent so far + recurring charges still to arrive + the line's usual everyday spending (its monthly average over the last complete months, leaving out one-offs and recurring charges) for the part of the month still to come. A bill already paid is not multiplied up. The share of the month that has passed is measured to the date your least up-to-date account's statement runs to, not today. With fewer than 3 complete months to learn from, the month-to-date run rate is used from a quarter of the month on; before that the pace says Too early. On track = projected within the limit. At risk = projected over by at least 10% and 50 EUR. Over = already more than the limit. Irregular = a line spent in only a few of the last months (a yearly bill, a repair): no everyday average is added, so the figure is what is already spent plus the recurring charges still due, and it never raises an alert unless the limit is already passed. No pace is shown for a month with nothing imported.

Yearly line: the amount is a YEARLY figure (insurance, a holiday). Each month a twelfth is the cash to set aside, but the limit is a rolling 12 months: the line is over only when what was spent in the 12 months ending at that month exceeds the yearly amount. The month a bill lands is measured against the yearly amount less the previous 11 months' spending, so the bill is covered even if nothing was set aside yet. There is no January reset. Months without imported statements count as nothing spent and are named in a warning.

Carry over: what a cost line under- or overspent in earlier months of the same calendar year moves into the current month (months with imported statements only). The variance is then against 'available' (planned plus carried). The carried amount starts over in January, but a window that spans New Year is still measured as what was carried in + everything planned in it - everything spent in it. Only applies to spending and debt lines.

Cash-flow forecast: where this month ends and the next months, deterministic, no AI. It starts from the date each bank account's latest statement runs to, places recurring charges (quarterly and yearly included) on their due dates, and adds income and everyday spending from the average of complete months (one-off rows left out). The balance line is a bank-account balance projection built from the latest stored balances; transfers to your own accounts, such as a broker, are not projected. A figure that cannot be worked out is shown as 'not available', never as 0.
Range: the low and high come from the smallest and largest everyday-spending month in the baseline, so it shows how much past months varied, not a probability.
Estimated Tax: Spanish IRPF savings-base tax on this plan's realised gains, based on current data and latest prices — an estimate, not a filing figure.
